Hello everyone, my name is Martínez Ceagalli. Tennis Australia has asked me to share my thoughts on a sport that, although it is experiencing rapid growth in many parts of the world, Paddle, I mean Paddle, has actually been around for several decades in many other countries. I've been involved with Paddle for more than 35 years and in this presentation I will try to set out some ideas which I believe are interesting for a better understanding of what Paddle is all about. However, first and foremost, I would like to thank Tennis Australia not only because of this invitation, but also because this is an organization that is going to be the responsible for guiding the development of Paddle. And without any doubt, education and the dissemination of specific content are a fundamental piece for ensuring that development. Furthermore, as a racquet sport, Paddle shares similarities with Tennis. For that reason, I will focus this presentation on the relationship between the two sports. Although, as you will see, Paddle is a distinctly different sport. So, let's get started. When I was young, I played tennis at a decent level, I would say. I became a certified coach in the professional tennis registry and worked as a tennis coach for several years, which was great because it's a sport I love. However, about 35 years ago I started playing Paddle in my home country of Argentina and I have been working to develop this sport ever since.

In this presentation, I would like to offer some advice to tennis coaches and players who are interested in trying Paddle like me. After many years of making mistakes, of which I am also proud, I have discovered that a very good way to understand Paddle is through its differences with tennis rather than its similarity. Excellent tennis coaches, so when I started teaching Paddle, I naturally adopted the same approaches, methodology and teaching styles as I had used on tennis court, making only a few minor changes. However, I discovered the threat of a single letter. Tennis can be a good source of resources for Paddle as long as we adopt them rather than simply adopting them. Before outlining some of the technical and tactical differences between the two sports, I will give you six tips on how to become a good Paddle player or coach in addition to being a good tennis player or coach. Use critical thinking, play as much as possible, watch lots of matches, educate yourself by doing research and seeking information, prefer doubt to certainty, make mistakes, talk about grips. The recommended grip for Paddle is the Continental grip. However, for certain shots or levels, the pair of Eastern grips, forehand and backhand, are also recommended. This is not only because in Paddle we volley many times in each point, but also because the contact points are very different from those in tennis.

In tennis, we try to hit the ball forward and high, whereas in Paddle, the contact points are often behind and low. Another reason for this difference lies in the types of spin that are most commonly used in each sport. Topspin is the most commonly used spin in tennis, while underspin is very important in Paddle. An important difference lies in the concept of the line of defense. In tennis, we try to prevent the ball from crossing a line, whereas in Paddle, we sometimes deliberately try to make it cross. The first decision a tennis player must make is whether to use the forehand or backhand, whereas Paddle players must also decide whether to use the bounce of the ball. This affects footwork among other things. Transitions from the baseline to the net and particularly from the net to the baseline are uncommon. A serve and volley, an approach shot, a lob or a passing shot could cause a forward transition. Only a lob would force us to back up in tennis. In that situation, it is not easy to restart a tennis point. Paddle is completely different. During a point, there can be many transitions in both directions for both couples. Furthermore, it is relatively easy to reset a point in Paddle. This is probably one of the simplest yet most difficult concepts for a tennis player new to Paddle to understand. Let's talk about lobs. In tennis, a lob is a specific shot and an alternative option.

In Paddle, however, it is a basic shot. In tennis, it is best executed with topspin. In Paddle, however, this would be a poor choice. To be honest, we often find matches with lots of lobs in recreational tennis rather boring. In Paddle, on the other hand, lobs are an integral part of the game and will feature in every point. This is another important characteristic of Paddle that we must accept when playing and when planning sessions and exercises as coaches. Now let's talk about volleys. Although volleys appear to be quite similar in tennis and Paddle, there are few significant differences. Firstly, in tennis, the volley is related to the definition of the point. This is why the volley involves a relatively simple technique that aims to put the ball out of the opponent's reach. Unlike in tennis, it is not possible to win a point in Paddle with a single shot. This is because of the number of rebounds that occur around the perimeter of the court, causing the ball to tend to return to the opponent's position. This creates technical and tactical differences compared to tennis volleys. In Paddle, we often add preparation and follow through to shots to generate underspin. Additionally, the concept of keeping the ball in play with volleys to set up the point often translates into open stance volleys. However, in Paddle, as in tennis, we also use the block volley in some circumstances.

In fact, many serve returns are made with these shots. In addition to the version that bounces on the ground, Paddle players must also master the version that bounces off the side wall. Attack and defense. Another consequence of the differences in net play between Paddle and tennis, although not the only one, is that there is no clear distinction in Paddle between attack and defense based on position on the court. In Paddle, you can attack from the back of the court and defend at the net. As with volleys, we need different overhead shots to play Paddle correctly. We need some to rally and set up the point, some to put pressure on our opponents and some to close out the point. These shots have different names, bandeja, bivorita, rulo, hook, por tres and por cuatro, among others. We also use different spins in the overheads such as side spin, flat and top spin and even under spin in the bandeja. How many types of overhead shots do you know in tennis? In addition, you should be prepared to hit your overheads several times per point. This is another major difference from tennis.
